This is a problem we have when you come from outside like I do, and I'm not so familiar with political life in the former Yugoslavia, so this is something which we get to know better over time. This is when we come to realise that the situation is an extremely complex one. You have just said now, you have just mentioned the Serbs from Croatia. Right. We know that Serbs lived in Croatia, and we know that there was quite a number of them. As part of this decentralisation of this new era that was to emerge, how did you intend -- at your level, how did you intend to settle the situation of the Serbs in Croatia? How was this going to occur? Were things going to develop favourably or not? How did you see things?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In all the talks and documents, the Serbs in Croatia were to be given all possible rights, guaranteed according to the highest standards of the United Nations and the civilised world; and in that respect, Your Honours, the Serbs, many of them lived in Istria, for example, around Rijeka, over 40.000 of them remained living there throughout the war as completely equal citizens, or in the city of Zagreb, for example, where there were 70 to 80.000 Serbs. Some of my actor friends and writer friends, they were Serbs, and throughout the war they lived normally as citizens of Croatia without any dilemmas. So here we're talking about organisation of the Serbs in areas which were supposed to be annexed to Greater Serbia. That is to say, the rural areas, Kordun, Glina, Knin, which is where there were just a small number of Serbs, albeit on a large territory, and that's where Serbian propaganda focussed on. They accepted weapons, and if you want me to, I can tell you about this at length. But anyway, the Serb question in Croatia, from the very outset, from the resolutions passed, from the constitution of the Republic of Croatia that was passed, was resolved in the manner in which the civilised world does it at the highest level. So when I say "civilised world," I mean from the United Nations and everybody else, they wrote down how it should be, and that is how it is today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... telling us, and this is under oath, and when I say "under oath," I mean that because it's very important, and this is why I'm using this expression. You're telling us under oath that the Serbs in Croatia took weapons, took to weapons, and since they took weapons, they took them by themselves or were they teleguided from outside?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not going to say all Serbs, and that's what I've been saying. It was a relatively smaller number of Serbs, but in areas that were rather large and not densely populated, they received weapons from the Yugoslav People's Army. And in some places they took control of the police stations, such as Martic in Knin, and they simply armed themselves and said they were not going to obey the Croatian state -- or, rather, the Croatian republic any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. You explain what happened, but I must also tell you that if we had a Serb in front of us, Serbian person, we would ask him and he would say the opposite. He would say that they took to arms because they felt an aggression, they felt attacked by Croatians. Where is the truth?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, when you say jeopardised or under threat, then the next question should be where, when, and by what law? Where, when, and under what law? Nowhere, never, and under no law. Where were the Serbs under threat, the 40.000 Serbs living in Istria and so on? Where were the 80.000 Serbs in the city of Zagreb being put under threat, in Varazdin? Let them give me a shred of evidence. Among my colleagues, actors, for example, one of them -- one of whom led a group, which was called the Cultural Battalion, walking around and that was led by a Serb. They were members of the party, they were in the government, and they were members of parliament. And Mr. Tudjman, and I know that myself because I took part in all this, he would call them up and talk to the leaders. He called -- he talked to Milan Babic. He told him to come to Zagreb to hear what he had to say. And in the Glina and Knin districts, full autonomy was proposed which means the right to their language. Well, all this is written down in the constitution of the Republic of Croatia, Judge Antonetti. There were always stories put out by the Serbs. They always said they felt threatened, they fell under threat, without providing any evidence. Of course they felt threatened because they were going to lose the privileges that they enjoyed for 40 years. That is true, privilege to -- the privilege to take my money, that I wasn't allowed to speak in my own language and that somebody could throw me in prison whenever they felt like it and to have their own army. That, yes, so if that's being under threat, and jeopardy --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You therefore go to Slovenia in the framework of the reporting you were doing -- you were making. What did you see with your own eyes in Slovenia concerning the Serbs? How will things develop according to you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Yugoslav People's Army quite simply wanted to come out to the borders, because Slovenia had previously said that they were independent and that they would take up their positions along the borders which meant to deny Yugoslavia. And then the Serbs in Yugoslavia felt in jeopardy, and then they acted there with arms, with weapons, but it was clear to everyone that in actual fact, although there were some people dead, people dead on both sides, there was shooting and planes were flying, but anyway, it was all done in such a way as to allow Slovenia to secede from -- allow Slovenia to secede from Yugoslavia. And once the Slovenes had a bit of a fight with them, the war was stopped and the Yugoslav People's Army withdrew from Slovenia and transferred its troops and tanks and weapons to the territory of Croatia and in part to Bosnia-Herzegovina. And I showed you the film, unfortunately another version, when the Croats stood in front of tanks in Zagreb, and I happened to be there myself, and we prevented them from going from the barracks towards Slovenia. I was against that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, you say that the war stopped. The war was stopped by the international community? My question may be a bit leading, but --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The international community did not stop the war. Unfortunately, the international community stopped nothing, and the war did not stop of its own accord. It stopped by a previous decision on the part of Serbia -- or, rather, the Serb leadership saying that they weren't interested in Slovenia. And their territorial claims did not go towards Slovenia but only towards Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina if we look to the west.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. So thanks to you we are making progress. We are making some headway. Now we know that after the conflict with Slovenia the JNA redeployed its troops in Croatia and in Bosnia-Herzegovina. When you saw this, what was your reaction, and what were you going to do at your level?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did what I intended to do. When in 1991 the aggression against the Republic of Croatia opened -- started openly by setting up barricades along the roads and taking control of the police stations and the complete arming of the Serb population in the areas to which I'm referring, I wanted to join the National Guards Corps, but they rejected me because I was too old. There were people who were far younger than me, some younger guys. And then on the 3rd of September, 1991, I happened to meet a friend who was going to Sunja, leading some reserve police force, and I said, "Can I go with you?" And he said, "Yes, you can." And that's how I came to go and fight as a volunteer, fully convinced that the situation would resolve itself only by us not losing the war, only if we didn't lose the war. And I was fully conscious of the fact, and we've discussed this with many people from the international community, that the international community and all the main protagonists wanted to retain Yugoslavia and allowed the Serbs to do everything they wanted from toppling the constitution and other things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Personally, I'm looking at paragraph 15 of the indictment. I will read to you the beginning: "Between the 18 November 1991 and April 1994, several people started a joint criminal enterprise." We'll come back to this. If I understand rightly all this, in September 1991 you left of your own accord in the region of Sunja to fight. This is a choice you made personally. It's not Mr. Tudjman who told you to go there and even less [indiscernible] or Susak. It's, say, yourself who went as a voluntary without taking part, maybe, in any form of enterprise. It was an individual personal act which was based on the fact that you were a voluntary. That's what you're telling us.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I belonged to the undertaking of Croatian volunteers and Serbs and Muslims, because in Sunja there were considerable numbers of all three. Mostly Croats, that's true. Anyway, I belonged to the movement of volunteers defending their country. Neither Tudjman, Susak wasn't the minister, Bobetko hadn't become a part of it yet. So I, through my own free will went to fight as a combatant, as a fighter. I had no rank. I just had my own weapons that I had procured earlier on. I had a Schmeisser dating back to World War II which was a present from a friend from Germany. That was before, because I talked to him several times and we socialised and discussed what was going to happen, and he said, "Here's a weapon for you." And I managed to bring that weapon in in the car --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Overlapping speakers] [Previous translation continues] ... the fight at Sunja, you are going to stay how much time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] [Previous translation continues] ... in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, I was too fast. I repeat. You were going to fight at Sunja? For how long are you going to stay in Sunja?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Six months and perhaps seven or eight days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. So you will stay there until February -- February or March 1992.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. I stayed until the 10th, I think it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: 10th of March, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. Therefore, under oath you're telling me that you were in Sunja until March 1992 without having met any of those who are mentioned in the indictment as being members of a joint criminal enterprise. That is to say, Tudjman, Bobetko, Susak, all those you did not meet. At Sunja, what you actually are doing? You are a private, a commander? What are you doing in Sunja actually?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've expanded my answer somewhat, Judge Antonetti. When I left, I just told my wife -- I said, "Darling, I'm off. I won't be subjugated." And in the first -- I was a soldier for the first five or six days, and then because of my involvement and because they assessed probably my capabilities, they appointed me commander. So up until the 10th of March, 1992, I was the commander of the defence of Sunja. And this extended towards Jasenovac later on. May I be allowed to state that I met Dr. Franjo Tudjman --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- commanding? You were designated as commander by whom? Who appointed you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was appointed to that post by the commander of the entire area from Sisak --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: You are again and again overlapping each other. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Judge Prandler is right. Sorry. I interrupted you. You said you met Franjo Tudjman and then I started speaking. I'll tell you why, actually, because I didn't want to start this question of Franjo Tudjman. What I wanted to know was who appointed you as a commander, and this is the answer I want. You were elected as a commander?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was appointed commander by Bozo Budimir, the commander of the operation zone to which Sunja belonged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bozo Budimir.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under whose authority was he?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time his superior officer was General Tus, the Chief of the Main Staff of the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So General Tus, you knew him?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I met General Tus later on. Not then but later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, let's go back when I interrupted you. When you were in Sunja, did you meet Tudjman, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: A little before Christmas, the Christmas of 1991. Gojko Susak called me up and said -- and asked me whether I could come to Zagreb. I went to Zagreb, and then he said to me -- well, there was a problem of weapons, and he happened to procure some 30 rifles for me somewhere. And I said, "All right, Gojko. I don't suppose you just called me up to take over 30 rifles. What else is there?" And he said, "Well, you should -- you ought to go and see the president. You ought to go and have lunch with the president." I said, "Well, the president is my commander. He can only order me. He can order me to do what he wants and I will obey." Now, since our relations were somewhat different because of our party activity, I went to have lunch with Dr. Tudjman, and we discussed the situation, and he said that we had to take on ranks because people were coming in from outside. I wasn't very favourable to that idea of getting a rank, I and colleague Medimorac, but his arguments prevailed. And he said, "All right. It doesn't mean anything to you, but once foreign officers turn up," and there was preparation for the cessation of hostilities and recognition of Croatia, "These foreigners aren't going to talk to anybody without a rank." So I was given the rank of colonel, and that was my first rank. I mildly objected because I thought the war would end and then I wouldn't be able to be a film director anymore, because it wouldn't be Praljak directing, it would be Colonel Praljak or whatever. So those were the reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this dinner you had with Mr. Tudjman before Christmas 1991. According to you was this to give you a rank, or was Mr. Tudjman trying to use you as a trump for the future since you had been a candidate against him? Was it a manoeuvre to try and recuperate you, to lure you, telling you you will be colonel or general in order to flatter you, because he certainly had other fish to fry than to look after you while you were in Sunja. You were not even number -- you were known, of course, but he certainly had other generals at hand, or other colonels. Now, with hindsight, how did you -- how do you remember this dinner? Was it a way of trying to make you join his political orbit?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judge Antonetti, Your Honour, I did belong to the political circle around Franjo Tudjman. So I shared all his basic ideas in that respect. There were some minor differences, perhaps, because he asked me, "What do you now think about some of your political moves and so on," and I said, "You were quite right and I was wrong," on some particular matter. And Dr. Franjo Tudjman and all the people who worked with me knew that you couldn't persuade me to do anything I didn't want to do, and in that respect, well, that was it. And thirdly, Dr. Franjo Tudjman respected me as far as I know as an individual and also because of my success on the battle-field, because Sunja was a very difficult theatre of war, and in the organisational sense, and in every other sense it was a very difficult battlefront. The most difficult perhaps on all of Croatia. And this was on television. There was broadcasting about it. Papers wrote about it. And in that respect I gained quite considerable authority. And it was an open discussion, and I was a Croatian soldier, a Croatian volunteer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You just said that all these questions were touched upon. Did he touch upon with you the question of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the situation of Croats in Herzegovina? Did he touch upon this subject or not?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke more about Bosnia-Herzegovina myself than Dr. Tudjman did, because I claimed, and I said this to my commanders in Sunja, you have the statement, I said that Croatia -- that what happened in Croatia, that is to say, the BH Army attack and what we called -- well, the Yugoslav People's Army against Croatia and what we referred to as the Chetniks or rebel Serbs, that that would be very weak compared to what was going to happen in Bosnia-Herzegovina, not a patch on what was going to happen in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And I say with full scientific certainty that I knew what was going to happen in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I knew exactly what was going to happen as soon as the Serbs saw that they had not achieved their plans in Croatia. And there was a thesis that I support that if an aggressor does not achieve his goals --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to go into the heart of matters, because if we go on like that we can be here for weeks, and Judge Prandler, of course, is looking at the timing. So I would like to go directly to the matter in hand. For my part I'm trying to determine exactly at what date there was the constitution of an enterprise. I'm not saying a criminal enterprise but an enterprise which could have consisted in what Mr. Tudjman and others may have had territorial views on some parts of the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in particular on Herzegovina, on the Posavina, or the Banovina. So I'm trying to identify in order to have a precise date of the beginning of the project, a precise date. Now, you're telling me that this -- at this dinner you spoke about Herzegovina, but did Mr. Tudjman tell you, "Slobodan Praljak, we must send troops in Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We must -- well, the Croats who are in Mostar, Stolac, and Capljina or other places have to take political control of their own area, their own region. For this I need you"? Did he say anything like that to you or not? I repeat that my question is always asked because you are talking under oath, answering under oath.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour Judge Antonetti, I know that I'm talking under an oath. In a certain way, I'm very -- I'm finding it very hard to answer these questions, because this is the ultimate absurd. It was just the other way round. Dr. Franjo Tudjman, in all of his appearances, showed optimism, and he believed much more into the institutions of the international community. He believed that the international community would realise what was going on and that in one way or another they would stop something that was as clear as daylight, and that was that the Serbs were armed and that they had a plan, and that was the plan. That was the only plan. Your Honour Judge Antonetti, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, during this dinner he did not talk to you about this. He did not tell you, "I have a plan, and this is what we're going to do." He never told you anything like that, did he?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not for a moment. I claimed and I said, "President, they will attack Bosnia and Herzegovina. They are fully braced for that. They will break us apart, and then they will carve the whole area down to Split. They have deployed forces." We knew everything, for crying out loud. All the documents are at your disposal to that effect. And what is going to happen there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you told him this, what did he answer?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: "They will not, Praljak. France, America, they understand. They have seen what was going on. We will be recognised. Once we are recognised, then this and that and the other," and so on and so forth. On the one hand, he was a very realistic person and he knew things, more or less; and on the other hand, he expressed his expectations. He wanted somebody to say to the Serbs in office, "Enough." Although he realised that they had been allowed to attack Croatia and that they would equally be allowed to attack Bosnia-Herzegovina, because nobody in the world paid anything but lip-service against that. Zimmermann, America, French diplomacy, Mitterrand, everybody was in favour of Yugoslavia. They wanted to resolve the problem not with constituting five or six more states but to give the Serbs a carte blanche for what they wanted to do. And this was not a joint criminal enterprise. It was a joint political enterprise to preserve Yugoslavia by allowing the Serbs to do what they were doing at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. So if I understand you properly, in Mr. Tudjman's mind he was hoping -- he had all hopes in the international community, and he thought that when the Republic of Croatia would be recognised the problems would disappear just like magic. That was his point of view. Your own point of view was more foreseeing a catastrophe, war to come because the Serbs were going to attack. That is the way you saw things, may I summarise the situation in this way, at the end of 1991?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so. As I say, I claimed that the Serbs would attack and that the recognition of Croatia within its boundaries was just paying lip- service to the whole thing and that it would drag on for years after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to understand better, and this may be useful for other people. If I summarise what you have said and if I make a mistake, don't hesitate to tell me. So you go back to Sunja, and you're going to stay there until March 1992. What do you do after that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know that a document that was signed in January, and that was some sort of a cease-fire. On the 15th of January, the European Community recognised Croatia, and then at the time we all thought that war was more or less over. There was some sporadic shooting on the front lines, but in one way or another Sunja became calm and I returned to Zagreb. And I accepted the offer to become the assistant minister of Defence Minister Gojko Susak for information and psychological activities, or information and political activities, as you will, and immediately upon that, maybe a day or two after, I became the assistant minister of defence of the Republic of Croatia for IPD and I assumed the duties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, you are assistant minister of defence in charge of IPD. You take up this position. If I understand correctly, at this point in time you become part of the Croatian military apparatus.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What prompts you to belong to the apparatus? Is it the alarming situation? Is it the fact that you would like to please your friend Susak? Is it because you would like to experience something new in your life? What is the decisive factor that triggers this commitment?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The job was still not finished. The job in question was the organisation of the Croatian state. The Croatian state was recognised on paper, but nobody really cared what was happening in the occupied territories, how and when the occupied territories would be liberated, and what was happening with the killings of Croats in the occupied territories, what was happening with the refugees in Croatia. All of that was of no concern -- or, rather, not of -- of not much concern to the international community. There were just hundreds of reports, hundreds of meetings involving ministers, ambassadors, but those were all in vain. Those were futile meetings where everybody just spoke their minds, but nobody wanted to really think about how to resolve the problem. And the only way the problem could be solved was by respecting the basic principles of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must address the structure of the enterprise which in the eyes of the Prosecution is criminal because crimes were committed. So we shall discuss all the people that I mentioned and whom you know one way or another. Let me get to the first person, Franjo Tudjman. You discussed him already at length, but there are also other aspects that need to be highlighted. You're assistant minister of defence in charge of IPD. Did you have the opportunity to meet Mr. Tudjman on several occasions?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On several occasions I met with him in the VONS, in the Council for National Defence to which I was appointed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you meet him on several occasions as well as member of the National Defence Council. You meet him because he headed the army or because he is the president of the republic or because he's both of these?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour Judge Antonetti, the two were so mixed in the war it was really difficult to draw a line between the military commander and the president of state, because all things were rather intertwined. So I wouldn't be able to -- obviously we met more because of some military issues. However --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From April 1992 onwards, in your position as a military you meet Mr. Tudjman. In the conversations you have with him, well, one of the important issues be addressed, i.e., the situation of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We discussed that issue. I was the one who imposed them on Dr. Tudjman rather than the other way round. Especially I did that through Mr. Gojko Susak, because I kept on claiming what I was claiming from the very outset and which eventually be -- came true. What I claimed was there would be a complete bloodshed in that territory and that all the forces, all the thoughts were already in position, and what ensued was just the implementation of all that. All the negative energies were already at play, and one could do nothing but watch how they will be materialised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Over the next few days I will have the opportunity to address the documents that relate, on the one hand, to the meetings of the National Defence Council, which you took part in, and on the other hand, the presidential transcripts in which you are mentioned, and other meetings which you attend. I will be able to get back to these documents afterwards. I will not address them now, because at this stage I had not intended addressing these documents. I'm trying to qualify the participants in this enterprise. As far as you are concerned, you have told us that this person was an historian. Do you think he had a good understanding of the international situation, of the situation of the Republic of Croatia, of the situation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and of the ambitions of the Serb leaders in the future? Was he an enlightened person, or with hindsight, could you say that he had a few shortcomings?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: President Tudjman was a very well-educated man, a very realistic person. He was completely devoted to democratisation. His idea was for the territory of the Balkans to be organised similarly to Scandinavia. He wanted Bosnia and Herzegovina to look like Switzerland. He had a complete overview. He was well informed. He was a reasonable person, a realistic person. His only shortcoming, which arose from his desire, wish, or strive, was that he placed too much hope in the politicians of the West. France, America, and all these politicians and states had different projections, views. There was jealousy among themselves, and they did not engage in our war in the way they could have. And if they had been engaged from the very outset as they could have, if they so wanted to, they could have stop the war entirely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, what I'm getting at is this presidential system in which President Tudjman was at the head of the army and president of the republic. Was he a very powerful man in political terms, or like any parliamentary system, was he at the mercy of the political majority? You have told us that all the parties had the same vision. Was he dependent on his political allies, or did he embody, like any system, was he the personification of absolute power?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour Judge Antonetti, he was not omnipotent [Realtime transcript read in error "not only omnipotent"] in political terms and he did not want to be omnipotent in human terms. There was a parliament which comprised other parties as well. There was a constitution that he had to abide by as well as everybody else. There was a government at the time, the government of national unity, and the ministry and that government came from all the parties save for the HSP. Franjo Tudjman wanted to rally people, all Croatian forces, the forces of civil society of Croatia. During the times of war you shouldn't forget that in the Croatian army there were people from Hungary, Slovakia, Serbia, Muslims. Everybody who wanted and who recognised the constitution of the Republic of Croatia, the constitution, I'm saying, and everybody who understood what this country was to become, he -- Dr. Franjo Tudjman wanted to rally all those people around a very broad political platform. In other words, all the things that in normal democracies, the arguments around tax systems and stuff like that, were not important at the time. We first had to lay the foundations of the state so the topics of war, armament, embargo, the nonfunctioning of the institutions, who to choose or appoint as ambassador, those were all new issues on the agenda, and it took time for those issued to be resolved. There were a lot of such problems, the functioning of the police, the health system. All the institutions were new. They were weak. They were underdeveloped. And a positive selection that normally takes years had not been implemented, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would like to hear a little clarification. Mr. Praljak, you have said, and that is on line 60 -- page 68, line 23: "He was, Mr. Tudjman, not only omnipotent in political terms," and so on. Did you really want to say that he was omnipotent in political terms, because what you explained afterwards rather suggests that you wanted to say something else.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The other way round. He was not. I said that not only was he not omnipotent in political terms, he did not want to be omnipotent. He talked to everybody on all topics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I guessed so, but I wanted to clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, I shall fine tune my question. If we assume that Mr. Tudjman wanted to form a Greater Croatia either by annexing territories or by joining up with other territories, I'm not going to go into the detail of this, if this was a personal ambition of his, was he able -- from a political standpoint and given the state of the constitution, was he able to impose his vision on others?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not in constitutional terms, not in political terms. If we start from that assumption, Franjo Tudjman could not implement that without the consent of the parliament. There should have been a 66 per cent vote in the parliament. He could not have done that without the consent of the government even if he had the power to do so, which he didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, before we move on with our question, I would like to ascertain something. Have you read the indictment in your own language? Have you read the Prosecution's pre-trial brief in your own language? Have you read all of the presidential transcripts chaired by Mr. Tudjman? Have you read all the documents which mention your attendance? Is this something which you are familiar with?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read the presidential transcripts. I know about the opinion and the presidential transcripts first-hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For your information, the Prosecutor's pre-trial brief was not translated into Croatian. The Prosecution doesn't have to translate it and it didn't. The general himself could not read it. He could read the indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I did not read the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, this is a question for you. You know that the pre-trial brief is an extremely important document. Mr. Kovacic, you didn't feel it was necessary to have this document translated so that your client was familiar from A to Z with the Prosecution's case?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That it should be translated we hoped that we would have it received, because there were discussions about that, but that was some five years ago, but I'm sure that we discussed the topic with our client. We discussed the positions of the Prosecution not only in the pre-trial brief but in other documents. You know that Mr. Praljak was actively involved, and he came to the two Status Conferences himself, and he was well informed. However, my objection went to the fact that he himself could not read that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I will share with you some passages of the pre-trial brief because I want to know what your position is, but I must tell you that I'm somewhat surprised by the fact that you did not get this document in your own language. This may be a shortcoming in our rules if one feels that the pre-trial brief, which is also part of the indictment, is not translated for an accused into his own language. This is a shame. It's a shame that no one has thought of that. But you have told us that you have not read it in your own language. We can't do much about it. Let me get back to Mr. Tudjman. You told us a while ago that he was unable to promote a personal action without addressing the intricacies of the Croatian constitution, which I'm sure you're more familiar with than I am. Could he, if he had the majority in parliament and if the Croatian people did not agree with him, could he have been out-voted? According to the Croatian constitution at the time, was it possible for an elected president to step down if his political project did not meet the approval of his people and his electorate?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour Judge Antonetti. The Croatian constitution is very precise. I subscribed to it to its every part. At that time, Franjo Tudjman on three or four occasions ran for office. He expressed very clear political views and positions. He won in the elections. His removal is prescribed by the constitution by way of referendum, by a vote in the parliament. The Croatian constitution guarantees a very high and precise system of democratic decision-making similar to the one that exists in your country, I believe. And let me now answer your question. Your Honour Judge Antonetti, I never read the indictment to the despair of my Defence counsel, especially Mrs. Pinter, for a very simple reason, because I have nothing whatsoever to do with the indictment, and I revolt after the third or the fourth page. I become nauseous and my blood pressure rises to the extent that my health becomes -- becomes jeopardised, and I refute the indictment in its entirety because it has nothing whatsoever to do with the reality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This is understandable. And this is what you are telling us, for a number of reasons you did not want to scrutinise the indictment. Had you done it, however, Mr. Praljak, you would have been able to better state your case, because this is an extremely important document.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I answer questions, I know what I did, and to be honest with you, I would not accept for my guilt to be proven beyond any reasonable doubt. I would rather subscribe to the following: If there is an iota of a reasonable doubt that I belong to a joint criminal enterprise or personally committed a crime, please try me, convict me, and I will subscribe to that. Find an iota of doubt, but don't say everybody set fire, and when Praljak could not pull out everybody who was on fire out of that fire, then it's a different story. That's not something I would subscribe to. I would not subscribe to the guilt because you didn't do what we think you should have done or you could have done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, this is not what we are discussing. The Trial Chamber has not deliberated on this matter. I can't say that we are light years away from this, but I'm trying to understand gradually what you are charged with, and I'm trying to better understand what you are telling us. This is why I'm putting questions to you. Unfortunately, time flies and I have to make a break. We shall now have a 20-minute break unless my colleague would like to add something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I don't think we can leave without response. Your request, Mr. Praljak, to be convicted if there's the slightest doubt of your innocence, things do not work like that. You are only convicted if there is no doubt about your guilt. So you will not change the law, and you have to put up with it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know, Your Honour, but what I was saying was that I was prepared even to subscribe to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're now having a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we resume our hearing. Mr. Praljak, during the break I perused again the memorial, and I will read you something and you'll tell me. It's paragraph 24, pre-trial brief. I will read it very slowly. "During a meeting in Zagreb on the 27th of December, 1991," that is to say, two days after Christmas. You told me you had met Tudjman before Christmas. So this is a specific period. This is very close for the date, "Franjo Tudjman summarised the objective of the common -- joint criminal enterprise, and he stated," I quote what Mr. Tudjman is supposed to have said, but I will specify that there is no footnote, so nobody knows where the Prosecution got this quotation for. They will certainly research it and will let us know later where they found this, but I'm going to quote what is written here. This is what Tudjman would have said. Listen: "It is time for us to take the opportunity, to seize the opportunity, to unite the Croatian people inside borders as wide as possible." This is what Mr. Tudjman would have said in December 1991. Therefore, Mr. Tudjman would have said, and I'm using the conditional tense, that from his point of view it was necessary to seize the occasion to unite the Croatian people in borders as wide as possible. What do you have to say to this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I read all this and I know what was discussed. The matter in hand was this, it was very simple: Franjo Tudjman isn't speaking about borders here but about the nation, the people, a united people. And only one thing was clear, and that was that the borders of the republics are inviolable, signed by the United Nations, repeated a hundred times. However, if the Muslims, the leadership led by Alija Izetbegovic, which was reaching agreements with the Serbs and negotiating with the Serbs, wanted to annex Bosnia and Herzegovina to Yugoslavia, to conjoin it with Yugoslavia, then and only then would the Croats of Bosnia-Herzegovina wish and desire and have the right not to go to Yugoslavia within as broad as borders as possible. We do not want to go to Yugoslavia. Only under that condition, mathematically speaking, a necessary condition, a necessary condition, a historical agreement, and I presented it to you here, about the fact that Mr. Izetbegovic wanted to unite the Muslims of whom there were 2.300.000 in Bosnia, 2 million in Kosovo, in Sandzak so many, in Macedonia so many. So because of his nation, his people to want to conjoin with Serbia, we would not agree to that. That was the sole fact within that whole story and nothing more than that. I claim that today, too, that a sovereign nation, a constitutive -- a constituent nation has the right to decide not to join a state it doesn't want to join if it is a constituent nation and a sovereign nation and not a national minority under the constitution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you knew about this sentence, and you have explained to us what the interpretation is to be given to this sentence from your point of view. Now, going back to Mr. Tudjman -- excuse me. My colleague --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would like to elaborate a little bit. Mr. Praljak, we have a quotation in English. I don't know exactly what the translation was. Are you saying -- are you doubting that Tudjman ever said something like that, or do you accept that this is or may be a correct rendering of a sentence said by him?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judge Trechsel, that's a good question. I simply don't know whether Tudjman said it that way, but I do know, and I've read through all those documents again, he repeated it a hundred times, thousands of times. Anybody who wanted to listen, from Cutileiro. Bosnia-Herzegovina from Cutileiro was defined, and we said yes. And then Vance-Owen, we said yes; and Stoltenberg, said yes; and the recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina, yes; borders, yes. The demand that UN forces be placed at the border, that was asked, called for umpteen times. So always one and the same thing. Bosnia-Herzegovina, yes. The Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina need to get their right to self-government, self-administration either within a confederation or federation or canton or whatever. Mostly there was the example of Switzerland quoted. For goodness sake, there's Switzerland. Let's follow the example of Switzerland. But I don't know whether this quotation is correct, because sometimes a word is lost and it needn't always reflect the exact political position taken. That is why it is necessary -- yes, I apologise. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. We may come back to this if we -- we find the place where it's quoted from perhaps. I think we leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Maybe just for reference, this is a citation from presidential transcript which is already in evidence. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Praljak, let's go back to Mr. Tudjman. We know, because you told us today, and you also told us a few days ago, that you knew the son of Mr. Tudjman very well. Did you continue to have relations with him after you were indicted here?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: A friendly relationship, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the indictment was published, revealed with the name of Tudjman, what was the reaction of the Croatian political class in general?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: All those who, with the exclusion, that is, of a number, a small number of those who -- a negligible number, negligible number of people who -- who in that respect, just like the international community, took for granted the very bad information and speedy -- speedily disseminated information. Everybody else was absolutely astounded by the accusations and indictment and -- because of all the facts that I've said. You arm, you receive refugees and the wounded, and you help and assist in every way possible. You recognise Bosnia, et cetera, et cetera, and then somebody comes up and say, "You did all that to trick America," whereas in all the transcripts the basic problem -- our basic problem was to see what it is the international community wishes and how to adapt to their wishes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. General Praljak, I read, just as you did, transcripts. You have all the documents. You have all the papers. Clearly, but we'll come back to this in detail later, now I want to speak about the generalities, Mr. Tudjman discovered this Stupni Dol business, and the question of the destruction of the Old Bridge on Mostar, the transcript of Stupni Dol, not torpedo, which is the village. Stupni Dol, excuse me. Right. Everybody understood, I think. He discovered this and you can read this in the transcript. He didn't know about it. He discovered this later on, and all the questions he asks show this. Is it possible, according to you, that Mr. Tudjman might not have had a complete vision of the events which were unfolding in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the republic? Did his inner circle, his councillors, did they give -- tell him everything? Did he have first-hand information, or were they not well informed?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In certain aspects he received the wrong information. Otherwise, generally speaking, with umpteen talks with Izetbegovic people came to tell him what was going on, so in general terms, yes, he did -- he was informed. But neither him nor anybody from outside, nor you, Your Honours, nor the Prosecution, can fully understand what the situation was given that chaotic war situation. That is just not possible. So that everybody summarises this, reduces it, adapts it, and so on and so forth, and then you enter into the higher realms of thought, what ought to be done should have been done, and so on. However, the despair on the ground, death and so on, you can't understand that. Nobody can understand that unless they were there. Nobody can fully understand the situation unless they were there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the 8th of November, when you went back to Zagreb, was -- did Mr. Tudjman receive you immediately?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, not -- not straight away. Not immediately. We had some meetings later on. I think I attended some meeting of the VONS or whatever before I was relieved of my duties. So not immediately, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He received you how many weeks or months later?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't be sure, Judge Antonetti. I really can't answer that question. My memory doesn't serve me that well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How did you live through this period? You were the commander of the HVO under the authority of Mr. Mate Boban, but you were a Croatian, important person. When you went back to your country, Croatia, where you had responsibilities previously, Mr. Tudjman does not receive you immediately? How did you take this, or was it a way of disavowing you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in that respect, Judge Antonetti, I'm not vain. Somebody would look at it as an insult, but afterwards I was given the duty of -- I think this was afterwards. Was I? Was that afterwards, that I was a chief of his military cabinet, that I was his military advisor for a short time. I organised the archive of the Croatian army. And as you were able to see in one of my articles in the "Hrvatski Vojnik," Croatian soldier, I didn't mind what I did. But the fact is that as they were accusing me more and more of destroying -- having destroyed the Old Bridge and how this propaganda was disseminated, and the Old Bridge was destroyed precisely because of that propaganda, but as this propaganda was burgeoning, I became a persona non grata more and more, and I was, well, let's say less important, which I didn't mind privately speaking, but I did begin to mind because of the lies that were being put out. Now, as far as my departure down there is concerned, I wouldn't have looked for my replacement until the Muslim offensive in our area resulted in a downfall, that is to say, against the HVO. I was a good warrior. I was a good commander as far as was possible, so I wouldn't have given in there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You heard just as I did the American ambassador who came to bear witness just where you're seated now, and we understood that practically every day he was in contact with Mr. Tudjman either by telephone or directly. Therefore, the United States of America were scrutinising what was going on in the field. The same ambassador told us, I quote this from memory because I don't have the transcript here, he told us that the United States of America, through this ambassador, had asked for your departure as well as the departure of Boban, which had been the case. This is what he told us. According to your own knowledge of this matter of politics in Zagreb at the time, of the possible links or relationships between the states and Mr. Tudjman, was it possible that a country may ask that you be set aside as well as Mr. Boban, and that Mr. Tudjman couldn't do anything else than to give satisfaction to this great power?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In answer to your second question, let me give my answer using a transcript. Franjo Tudjman says: "If America decides to provide a corridor to Neum, to the Muslim side, then we can do nothing." And that is true. So the power and might that certain countries had in the area was such that they shaped the war, and I can say this six times under oath, how it was going to develop and so on. And so this war in Bosnia-Herzegovina was waged, among other things, as a propaganda campaign or a campaign for advertising detergent, for example. You pick an event that took place or didn't take place. The journalists inform about this event, and then you say you have to do that because we have this information. There is no information, Your Honour, in the world public arena about Doljani, Uzdol, and so on. There was no information about the offensive launched by the Muslim forces against the HVO for three months. And it is constantly being repeated that we are doing the attacking. I state that we never attacked. We defended ourselves. Now, as far as Mr. Galbraith is concerned, I don't know what he said about Franjo Tudjman or what he said to Franjo Tudjman, but I asked to be replaced before Stupni Do, and I have nothing to do with Stupni Do. That's number one. And the second point is this: I think that the animosity on the part of Mr. Galbraith towards me was of subsequent development because I spoke up publicly when he held a public rally, when he spoke in Slavonski Brod in the main square there as if it was a local region in America. Well, we're not a banana state for a statesman, foreign statesman, to make public speeches. And then he said, "Why are we hearing from this destroyer of the Old Bridge?" So it's enough to be an American and of course backed up by the most powerful country in the world. I'm not interested in those powers. What -- it can be whatever power and might they like. It's not true that I was replaced down there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, another question which I could have asked before but I ask you now. You told us a while ago you were in charge of the IPD. So you're somebody who knows the media. You know the power of the media, the role of information, especially during wartime. Therefore, if -- you were chosen for this post, certainly because of your personal qualities at the time in this field. Now, how is it that you, on the 8th of November, you hear about what happened in this village, how is it that at that specific moment you didn't make a communique as a commander of the HVO that you heard that these events happened and that you immediately ordered an inquiry? Why didn't you do this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, Your Honour Judge Antonetti. However, the problem of advertising, or as we say in modern times propaganda, is the problem of quantity. It's not just one -- or PR. It's not one piece of news. When you advertise Coca-Cola, you send out these advertisements 500 times a day over all the television channels. After the Old Bridge I came to the television station and said, "For the finger of one of my soldiers I would have destroy the bridge," because a commander has to say that. But I did not destroy the Old Bridge. You know what this is like? It's like throwing a few grains of salt into the sea. They broadcast it over 30 television channels and keep repeating it umpteen times, but I say things just once and it's as if I never said it at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're telling me you did that and it was lost. You know better than anybody else, since you're a specialist and methods of reporting, you know that when there are pictures on CNN or Sky, you see the impact it may have. And Mr. Tudjman, we'll talk about it -- in several transcripts you'll see he speaks about this. When these dramatic events take place, maybe at your level it was necessary -- it would have been necessary to set the record straight, in particular for the international media who are going to hurry on this. Now, for the Old Bridge you said you did this. Okay. I'm taking your word for it. But for this village, what did you exactly do?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same thing, Your Honour. I don't know. In some interview I said no. Nor did I have any communication, nor did I issue orders, and after that we undertook everything prescribed by law, an investigation. We included the international community. We handed it over to the investigating judge. We said, "For God's sake, launch an inquiry." But stories are stories. Today wars are shaped through CNN. That is what we can read in any book on communications and PR. If CNN wants to wage war, you're going to have a war. They come in first, and then you just wait for the war to break out, from Baghdad onwards. So it's a question of power and might. And everything that you asked me I said and denied for as long as people wanted to listen to me, until I said I'm going to investigate into the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. Now, we'll leave Mr. Tudjman for a moment, and we will now speak about Mr. Susak, who is mentioned in the indictment. You told us Mr. Susak was one of your classmates. How could you define Mr. Susak, who was once defence minister? According to you, what were his qualities?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Susak was sabotaged by the services of the former state. In one occasion he was incarcerated in Mostar. He was detained there. My father found him there, took him out of the prison, gave him money to go home. Just like many others, he went to study in Rijeka, and when he could not stick it out anymore he emigrated to Canada, and that was in the 1960s, maybe in the 1968 or 1967. And when he returned, he was already shaped up by a democratic society. For 30 years he had been abroad. He left as a young lad, and he returned as a man of 46, and he had very clear democratic ideas in every possible sense of the word. And in that sense, our private and our official communication remained at a very enviable level. We talked about everything. I don't know that we had any disparaging opinions about anything. None whatsoever that I can think of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was he doing in Canada?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Canada he established, together with a group of people, the Croatian language department in Ottawa or in Toronto. I don't know exactly where. And he was the owner of a company and then a very big pizza parlor. That's how he made a living. But in addition to that he held demonstrations in front of the Yugoslav embassy with regard to some events in Yugoslavia. He expressed his positions democratically based on what he knew about Yugoslavia. And he also established the department of Croatian language in either Ottawa or Toronto. I can't tell you exactly where.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm asking you these questions, because in the indictment and in the pre-trial brief we don't have all this information. How can you, if you make pizzas and/or deliver them, how can become --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was possible for a very simple reason. The quality of his education was much higher than would be required by a pizza parlor owner. He did not make pizzas. He just owned the pizza place, and we're talking about two different things here, of course. I was a waiter, Your Honour, with three university degrees, and I did not become a general as a former waiter but as somebody who was familiar with 30 international wars in much better terms than many generals who have completed very high education in America, for example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When he returns from Canada to play a part on the military and political stage in Croatia, the Croatians who were in Zagreb or elsewhere who were there, did they accept the fact that expatriates came back and the fact that these people were very close to Franjo Tudjman and played or held prominent positions?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not become defence minister straight away. First he was a party member, and then he became the minister of immigration in the Government of the Republic of Croatia. Croatia has a huge number of emigrants. In addition to Poland and Ireland, Croatia is a country which experienced huge waves of emigration. In America there are over 2 million Croats of the first, second, and third generation, and that's only in America. That's what Mr. Susak became. And since the two of his predecessor -- predecessors did not go -- do a good job, Tudjman chose Susak. There were some shows of resistance against Gojko Susak because there was a structure in the HDZ which was a hard -- an element of hard-liners, Communists hard-liners like Mr. Manolic and some others did not gladly accept him, and those were the same people that had prosecuted him. He did not have anything against them. However, he would not be ill-treated by the people and the views that they upheld about Croatia. The soldiers, however, liked Gojko Susak because he was a simple person, because he was a normal person, because he perceived his job as a job that he dedicated his life to without any political ambitions, any ambitions to achieve a political career.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is always difficult to extract information from the dead. You met him on several occasions. What were his views on Herceg-Bosna, on Bosnia and Herzegovina, on the Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina? Did he have any personal views or was that not a problem in his eyes?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: For him and for me it was a problem, as it was for Franjo Tudjman, and all of us shared an identical position which is testified and documented by all sorts of documents. A, the recommendation of Bosnia-Herzegovina as an integral state and the boundaries of Bosnia-Herzegovina as they existed in the time of Communism. However, within Bosnia and Herzegovina, the three peoples had to agree as to how they would arrange their relations. And Muslims would not be the first, or Croats or Serbs. They had to agree as equals, because those peoples were equal under the constitution, and nobody was in a position to impose their unitaristic ideas as the Muslims wanted in order to achieve their Muslim state. The Serbs wanted the whole country to be integrated with Yugoslavia and that was also out of the question. We wanted a Bosnia-Herzegovina, as you could have seen from my statements given to the French, with our own kind of self-government. And if the two people could agree, and I'm talking about the Serbs and Muslims, and do differently, it was only then that we would request for the parts where Croats were a majority would not go where they wanted to go. That was our right. That was my position, his position, and that was the position of the Croatian state policy, the position of Franjo Tudjman as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Susak's deputy, since you were in charge of this IPD department, you knew him well, professionally speaking. The mere fact that you were his deputy and you were familiar with the workings of the Ministry of Defence. I'm trying to draw a parallel with Bruno Stojic and the Defence Department of Herceg-Bosna and the MOD of Herceg-Bosna. I'm trying to see whether this functioned in the same way or operated differently. As far as Mr. Susak is concerned, when a military operation was carried out, was it Mr. Tudjman who directed the operation personally, together with his Chief of Staff, or was it the minister of defence who said to Mr. Tudjman, "That battalion will go there. That unit will go there. This and that needs to be done"? What part does -- or did the minister of defence of the Republic of Croatia play at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The minister of defence of the Republic of Croatia -- or, rather, the ministry was modelled after Western states. In other words, the minister of defence looked after the armament, the procurement, the IPD, the personnel issues, and so on and so forth. But the staff or the army, to the extent that they needed -- with regard the salaries on mobilisation relied on the minister of defence. However, the minister of defence did not deploy the troops, did not plan operations, did not control operations. He was not in charge of any of that. This was the same thing between Mr. Stojic and myself. Mr. Stojic was in charge, as far as he could be, of the remuneration for the troops, the procurement of food and clothes, to put pressure on municipalities with regard to mobilisation when there was a shortage of men. He was also looking after health care, IPD assistance, and so on and so forth. And I was subordinated to Mate Boban when it came to the operations, when, how, with whom, and I did it with my associates, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To sum up what you've just said, I stand to be corrected, and I stress this, the Minister of Defence, Mr. Susak, was not competent in the field of military operations. He was there to provide equipment, to make sure that the IPD was operating properly, pay out salaries. If I understand correctly, these were administrative tasks. These were not operational tasks.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour. Minister Susak could -- I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since you drew a parallel with the ministers of defence in Western countries, I shall put a technical question to you. In Zagreb the minister of defence, I assume, was located in a building. In the building in which the Ministry of Defence was housed was there an operations room in which officers on duty plotted the units on the map in realtime? Was this something which was done or wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The ministry building had two floors occupied by the Main Staff of the army, and that's where they had everything that a body of that kind might need. That building did not contain the command of the Croatian Air Force. It was in a different building, and the command of the Navy was in Split.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was an operations room, but according to what you're saying, it was on line 22, page 89, it was in fact the Main Staff that managed this operations room.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as you know, did the minister of defence, you even sometimes when you were deputy minister in charge of IPD, did you ever go into the operations room to see what was happening on the map or did you never do this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're talking about the organisation as it should be. The minister of defence obviously had to be informed about any operation. You could talk about that with the minister of defence. You could not plan an operation without being aware of the number of troops available to you, whether you will -- will be able to replenish, whether there was enough ammunition, and so on and so forth. When it comes to the planning of any operation, the minister or his assistants were involved. Any minister -- any minister's assistant, the assistant for Medical Corps, for IPD, or SIS. The involvement is one thing, and the implementation is an entirely different thing. Once the operation is under way, it is military commanders who are in charge. The minister can also follow any operation because he receives requests from the commanders when they need things, and it depends on how the operation develops.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you yourself were commander of the HVO from July 1993 to the 8th of November, 1993, did it happen sometimes that you received a phone call from Mr. Susak, asking you what the situation was like, "Can I help you?" Did you receive phone calls providing you with the information or providing you with the way forward?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in the nature you describe, but there were talks, of course. I would call Minister Susak about certain issues and problems. On the 24th, I sent him a letter requesting two battalions of the Croatian army. I did not receive them, because our military situation was on the brink of disaster at that time. Then I had problems with the training of helicopter pilots, with one general of the Croatian army, and then I asked from Susak to intervene in that matter because that person was just unreasonable, and at the end of the day he did not have the right to do what he was doing. So on my side there were some requests upon Minister Susak for him to approve some men for the Main Staff, some volunteers, to let them go from the Croatian army. But you have all the documents to that effect, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have a presidential transcript. We shall get back to this because I don't have it before me right now, but after you left after November 1993, there is a meeting between Mr. Tudjman, Mr. Susak, and Mr. Bobetko during which clearly maps are laid out, and Mr. Tudjman is discussing where the various people are, and it's quite surprising to discover that Mr. Tudjman was very well informed on -- with what was happening on the ground since he gives the name of commanders on the ground, which means, according to this document, that Mr. Tudjman could be very well informed. And on seeing this document, I wondered how he could be made aware of all of this. This is why I put this question to you and asked you if you received a telephone call from Mr. Susak saying -- or informing you about what was happening in realtime, and you then answered by saying that sometimes you phoned him up because you needed reinforcements, and this is something which is mentioned in a number of transcripts. So what I'm interested in is a question set against the backdrop of the joint criminal enterprise. I wanted to know whether at Susak's level, Tudjman and Bobetko, of course, there was a follow-up in realtime of the military situation in Herceg-Bosna. That's what I'm interested in. What do you have to say to that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was nothing realtime, Your Honour. Probably every now and then they would receive information from somebody else. The information -- I'm familiar with the transcript and the talks. We provided this information at a meeting in early November in Split. The information was very clear and precise. Irrespective of the fact that the offensive had already been crushed, there was still a clear and present intent of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina to come to the borders of Bosnia and Herzegovina and -- and those in the direction of the sea, in the direction of Ploce. I am saying that at -- if they had succeeded at the time, the international community would have given the area from Neum to Prevlaka to Serbs. They would have given the area from Neum to Ploce to Bosnia, and nobody would have blinked an eyelid. I wanted for the offensive to be stopped -- put a stop to because it was against the Croatian people, and I asked for assistance from Croatia. Unfortunately, I did not receive that on the 24th. I received -- I repeated my request on the 5th of November, and you can see it in the transcript. What I'm saying is for them to give me at least two battalions. This is all I was asking for in light of the fact that we were dealing with aggression, with an intent to occupy territories after the agreement was reached with Serbs in the month of September. One cannot be viewed without the other. If the Muslims and the Serbs had agreed in the month of September 1993 that they would create two states in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Serbian state and the so-called Muslim and Croatian state without Croats, mind you, and that the right would be given to the Serbs to go to a referendum and leave that state, then, Your Honours, we are talking about aggression against the Croatian people in the Neretva valley and further down towards the sea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since you are familiar with all the presidential transcript, these questions are easy for you. You don't have to do any research work. We have a presidential transcript where clearly there's quite a heated discussion between Mr. Tudjman, Mr. Susak, and Mr. Bobetko on the subject of volunteers and the fact that the minister of defence was issuing decrees on the mobilisation of volunteers. Mr. Tudjman says that the international community and CNN, once they heard about this, would be in a political conundrum. So clearly Tudjman reproaches Susak for this, which means that I can now address the question of the volunteers. Was it Mr. Susak who had the idea of sending "volunteers" to Bosnia and Herzegovina, or did he only manage them from an administrative point of view?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour Judge Antonetti, it was not Gojko Susak. I believe that it was my idea originally. I believe so. In its ranks, Croatia had between 12 and 15.000 volunteers from Bosnia-Herzegovina, and when war stopped in Croatia and those who had fled from Bosnia-Herzegovina, there were tens of thousands of those, and those people didn't want to defend their homes. Under the constitution of the Republic of Croatia, and because of the fact that Mr. Izetbegovic did not want to sign a military agreement with the Republic of Croatia, one could not send the regular army to Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the only way you could do it was to send volunteers. You could offer them salaries, and that was offered to both Muslims and Croats who went to wager war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. You could offer them a rank, for example. You could offer them some other benefits and perks. Despite all of that, and in that transcript you can see that volunteers for the operation in Uskoplje which failed were only 400. Four hundred volunteers, not more than that, and that's how things fell through up there after my departure. And then in January 1994, I returned there again because the whole situation was poorly managed up there, and there was an imminent danger that the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina would break through towards Rama. And the lads called me, "Come back," and I did, because we defended ourselves. All I did was throughout -- throughout the war was to defend myself. We did not attack Serbs in Serbia, anywhere. We did not attack their villages. You can see it in the transcript. We defended Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Muslim and Croat people in the areas that we managed to defend, and we never made a difference between the two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is just about time to stop. We have a few seconds left. As work planned for tomorrow, I shall resume my questions and address the issue of Mr. Bobetko. Then I shall review the other co-accused, Mr. Prlic, Mr. Stojic, Mr. Pusic, Mr. Petkovic, to see what connections there were between these people, and Mr. Coric also, whom I had forgotten, what contacts you had with these people and how you got to know them. I shall address three cases which are mentioned in the pre-trial brief, Blaskic, Kordic, and Naletilic, who according to the Prosecutor are members of a joint criminal enterprise since they are, all three of them, quoted in the pre-trial brief. We shall spend quite a lot of time on each individual case, and after that I shall start reviewing the documents, and I shall start with the contested documents which, according to you, are forged documents. I hope my questions have not tired you too much. If you are tired, please let us know, but you have all night to recover, and we shall meet again tomorrow afternoon, since we will be sitting at a quarter past 2.00. That said, I have another hearing in another case in the morning. Mr. Karnavas, I believe you would like to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I'm not tired. I will answer any question even if it takes months. I would like this to take months.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, speaking of -- speaking of months, Mr. President, Your Honours, in light of -- in light of what you just told us, it would appear that you -- your questioning will continue for the rest of the week, just for scheduling purposes. That's number one. And number two, earlier when you mentioned a transcript when you spoke of volunteers, I assume that that was from memory, but when you get to the documents you will be referring to it for our purposes, for the record, just so we know exactly, you know, where to look for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very much so. Yes indeed. I said "volunteers." Yes, Mr. Stringer, you wanted to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, not about this particular issue. It has to do with the IC documents that the President inquired earlier today what the Prosecution position might be on filing its response to the IC document of the Praljak Defence, and we've conferred and they have filed their final IC list today relating to the documents that were used last week, and our proposal would be for the Prosecution to file its response to -- to all of those documents one week from today, next Monday. And if I could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. We'll talk about this between ourselves, and we'll let you know tomorrow if we agree. I don't know yet. We'll discuss it between ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I would like to say that this is very reasonable and seven days would be really appropriate. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I will consult my colleagues, see if we can go fairly fast and then we could perhaps give our decision immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. I consulted my colleagues, as you've seen. We have taken note of the fact that you asked for seven days. Defence thinks it is reasonable, the Judges also. So you are given seven days for this. There's no problem about it. Therefore, Mr. Praljak, no other questions. Therefore, good evening, and we will meet tomorrow afternoon. The Chamber is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 16th day of June, 2009, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: [The accused Prlic and Coric not present]
--- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.03 p.m.,
